captions.instagram:
What sets the rate of a reaction?

A tank of 400 molecules collides hundreds of times a second and counts every reaction, and the count lands on the Arrhenius equation. Test the "doubles every 10 °C" rule and find the one hill for which it is true. Then cook dal in Leh, powder marble, clean a car's exhaust with platinum and ask why diamonds last.

→ Molecules react only when they collide hard enough to get over a hill of energy.
→ Heat the gas and far more collisions clear the hill. The counted rate follows the Arrhenius equation.
→ "Rates double every 10 °C" is only true when the hill is about 53 kJ/mol. Lower hills gain less, higher hills gain more.
→ A pressure cooker holds water at 120 °C, not 100. That 20 °C makes dal cook about four times faster.
→ A solid reacts only at its surface. The same marble as powder gives off its gas many times faster than chips.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/rateclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What sets the rate of a reaction? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A tank of 400 molecules collides hundreds of times a second and counts every reaction, and the count lands on the Arrhenius equation. Test the "doubles every 10 °C" rule and find the one hill for which it is true. Then cook dal in Leh, powder marble, clean a car's exhaust with platinum and ask why diamonds last.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/rateclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/rateclear

In this video:
• Collide hard enough. Molecules react only when they collide with at least the activation energy Ea, and the right way round.
• A few degrees, a big change. "Rates double every 10 °C" is exact only for a hill of 53 kJ/mol near room temperature.
• Only the surface reacts. A solid can be hit only at its surface.
• A lower path over the hill. A catalyst offers another route with a lower hill and comes out unchanged.
• Where the simple rules stop. A rate is not one number: it falls as the reactants run out, and a tangent to the curve reads it at any moment.
